newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian coup leaves major companies in turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian coup leaves major companies in turmoil.

text.p: Most international companies in Cambodia have suspended operations and evacuated non-essential expatriate staff from the country following a coup and two days of fighting in Phnom Penh a week ago.

A hand-lettered sign on the iron gates outside the handsome, shuttered villa headquarters of the British American Tobacco (BAT) in the Cambodian capital on Friday read: "Staff and employees should return on July 14".
"They're all gone. I think they left Cambodia because of the troubles," said a lone watchman at the villa.
"Maybe some of them stayed in town but I haven't seen them. I am hoping the situation improves so they come back next week."
The BAT factory in Phnom Penh's western suburbs has suspended its cigarette manufacturing operations until the 14th, at least, leaving about 800 employees without work.

Reporters saw a number of BAT expatriate managers and their dependents leaving the city on Wednesday via a privately operated mercy flight, one of dozens which have ferried foreign nationals to safety since the capital erupted in fighting last weekend.
The Phnom Penh office of the accounting firm of Coopers & Lybrand was shuttered on Friday. Area shopkeepers said they didn't know when the manager would return.
Cambodia Brewery, which makes Tiger Beer, was also closed and its factory was down to a skeleton staff.
Many shops and virtually all banks remain shut in the city, out of a fear of general lawlessness.
Looting and robbery, much of it by government soldiers, continued after the weekend's fighting.

One company which is "trying to carry on with business as usual" is the local unit of Royal/Dutch Shell which was the first major oil company to return to the country after the Khmer Rouge era in the 1970s.
"We've evacuated two of our employees and a number of dependents and we are monitoring the situation day-by-day, hour-by-hour," said Duncan Shurrock, Shell's Phnom-Penh-based Operations Manager.
"We have a substantial investment in Cambodia. We're here on a long-term basis and if we can operate with no risk to our staff we will contnnue to do so."
Shell supplies fuel to filling stations, industrial concerns and hotels, mainly in Phnom Penh and the port of Sihanoukville.
With a tanker docked at Sihanoukville, Shell has begun running convoys of fuel trucks, without armed escort, back and forth to the port to bring product to Phnom Penh.
Shell's aviation fuel terminal in the capital suffered minor damage and was looted during fighting over the weekend, but fuel is now being supplied to Royal Air Cambodge airlines again.

Cambodian strongman Hun Sen, who ousted his co-prime minister Norodom Ranariddh in the coup, is hoping that multi-national companies with major investments in Cambodia will remain in operation here even if they don't care for his politics.
But the Cambodian economy looks set to pay a steep price for Hun Sen's ambition and the bill has already started to come due.
Major international donors, including the United States, have pledged to suspend aid donations to Cambodia, which currently total about 50 per cent of the annual budget.
Security worries and a sudden halt in funding have combined to cause many non-governmental (NGO) agencies to evacuate their non-essential staff.
The knock-on effect of this turmoil has been a suspension of investment and business activity, further hobbling what is already southeast Asia's poorest economy.
Jusuf Nawawi, general manager for Phnom Penh's Land Rover and BMW dealership, had contracted for a new half-million dollar showroom and garage in the city, but has now stopped the project.
He sent two British staff members to Vietnam for their own safety and is worried about a dozen Land Rovers sitting in a container on the docks in Sihanoukville.
"I have a lot of money invested in Cambodia but I must admit the situation is very unpredictable," Jusuf said.
"The British Embassy said they thought things were returning to normal but I'm not sure. There's no point in me being open now.
"Most of our sales and maintenance business is for Westerners, Europeans, and they've all left town.
"If the NGOs shut up shop there will be a very reduced demand for Land Rovers. As for BMWs, forget it."
